title: LiDAR Extrinsic and Intrinsic Calibration for a Public Service Robot: A Case Study at Wongsonegoro Hospital, Semarang

authors.name: Prof. Ir. A. Hidayat, Ph.D.
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Diponegoro University

abstract: Mobile service robots in hospital environments depend critically on accurate LiDAR calibration for reliable mapping and localization. Despite advances in scan-matching and sensor fusion, prior work often reports persistent extrinsic misalignments and beam-specific intrinsic errors when deployed in complex indoor corridors and dynamic public spaces [1][2][3]. We propose an integrated calibration pipeline, Hospital-LiCal, designed specifically for the Wongsonegoro Hospital service robot platform. The proposed method combines time-synchronization, hybrid ICP with point-to-plane weighting, and a pose-graph optimization that jointly estimates extrinsic transform and per-beam intrinsic offsets. Extensive experiments in multiple corridors and wards show that Hospital-LiCal reduces localization RMSE to $0.12\,\mathrm{m}$ and map drift to $0.32\,\mathrm{m/km}$, outperforming ICP-only and manual alignment approaches by 62% and 48% respectively. Calibration completes in a median 18 minutes on an Intel NUC (i7), and the method is robust to occlusions and partial scan overlap. The study provides engineering guidelines for real-world hospital deployments and open-source ROS packages and datasets for reproducibility.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Hospitals increasingly adopt mobile service robots for tasks such as delivery, guidance, and disinfection. These robots rely on LiDAR sensors for real-time localization and mapping. Precise LiDAR calibration is essential because small extrinsic misalignments or per-beam intrinsic offsets can produce significant mapping errors in corridors, patient rooms, and lift areas. In the Wongsonegoro Hospital deployment in Semarang, Indonesia, our public service robot encountered mapping drift and localization discrepancies that affected autonomous navigation and HMI reliability, motivating a targeted calibration solution (see Fig. 1 and Fig. 2).

Prior work has addressed LiDAR calibration in research settings using methods ranging from manual alignment to fully automated intrinsic calibration algorithms [1][2][3]. However, despite achieving strong results in controlled datasets, prior work suffers from limited robustness to time-synchronization jitter, sensor mounting variability, and dynamic occlusions typical of hospital corridors [4][5]. Many existing methods assume either perfect timestamp alignment or require controlled calibration targets, which are impractical during live hospital operations [6].

The research gap addressed here is the need for a practical, repeatable, and fast calibration pipeline that jointly estimates extrinsic transforms and beam-specific intrinsic corrections under realistic hospital constraints: limited downtime, human traffic, and mixed 2D/3D LiDAR hardware. Specifically, our work targets the Velodyne VLP-16 and Hokuyo UTM-30LX sensors mounted on the hospital service robot platform, operating on an Intel NUC with ROS-based software stacks. The challenge includes dealing with partial overlap, rolling shutters in timestamping, and multipath reflections near glass and metallic surfaces.

To address this challenge, we introduce Hospital-LiCal, a novel approach to LiDAR calibration for hospital service robots. The proposed pipeline is designed to: 
- Provide robust time synchronization and preprocessing steps to mitigate timestamp jitter and sensor bias.
- Perform hybrid point-to-plane ICP with per-beam weighting and per-beam offset estimation.
- Integrate pairwise transforms into a global pose-graph and perform nonlinear optimization to jointly refine extrinsic and intrinsic parameters.
- Offer validation tools and GUI controls for rapid on-site verification and safe deployment.

The main contributions of this work are: 
1) Hospital-LiCal, a complete calibration pipeline tailored for hospital service robots and validated at Wongsonegoro Hospital, Semarang. 
2) A hybrid calibration algorithm combining ICP and pose-graph optimization that estimates both extrinsic transforms $T$ and per-beam offsets $\delta_b$ concurrently. 
3) A public dataset and ROS tools for reproducible calibration and comparative evaluation. 
4) Extensive field experiments demonstrating a reduction in localization RMSE to $0.12\,\mathrm{m}$ and a median calibration time of 18 minutes. 
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section II reviews related work; Section III presents the system design and methodology including equations and software architecture; Section IV describes experiments and results at Wongsonegoro Hospital; Section V concludes with limitations and future work.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section reviews prior literature on LiDAR calibration, sensor fusion, and hospital robot deployments. The following subsections examine extrinsic and intrinsic calibration methods, time synchronization and system integration, and domain-specific deployment studies.

section2a.title: Extrinsic and Intrinsic LiDAR Calibration Methods

content.text: Early extrinsic calibration approaches relied on fiducial targets and planar surfaces to compute rigid transforms between sensors via closed-form methods [7][8]. ICP-based techniques improved robustness by using dense scan overlap and iterative refinement [9][10]. However, ICP-only strategies often converge to local minima, particularly when initialization is poor or when partial overlap occurs, as is common in narrow hospital corridors. More recent methods estimate per-beam intrinsic offsets, accounting for systematic angular and distance errors in multi-beam LiDARs [11][12]. These intrinsic models typically parameterize beam-specific range bias $\delta_b$ and vertical angle corrections $\epsilon_b$, and perform batch estimation using collected scans. Despite achieving low RMSE on benchmark datasets, such methods often assume accurate timestamps and controlled environments, limiting applicability in busy hospital settings. Works by Levinson and Thrun introduced probabilistic models for beam noise and per-beam calibration [11], while Zhang and Singh proposed robust plane-based calibration for multi-beam sensors [12]. These studies motivate our joint extrinsic-intrinsic formulation which integrates time synchronization and pose-graph constraints to handle dynamic conditions.

content.text: As shown in Fig. 1, a practical calibration architecture must include reliable time synchronization and data recording subsystems to provide the consistent inputs required by both ICP and beam-level intrinsic estimators. Despite achieving good numerical results in laboratory conditions, prior intrinsic-only methods suffer from non-negligible residuals once deployed [13][14]. Our method bridges this gap by incorporating pose-graph constraints and hospital-specific validation steps.

Accurate timestamp alignment across LiDAR, IMU, and odometry is crucial for meaningful scan association. Network time protocol (NTP) and PTP (Precision Time Protocol) can reduce clock skew, but hardware and driver stacks create residual jitter that degrades calibration [15][16]. Methods to handle synchronization include software interpolation of poses, hardware PPS (pulse-per-second) signals, and robust synchronization modules in ROS [17]. In hospital deployments, we found that software-based time alignment using interpolation with bounded uncertainty provides a pragmatic compromise when hardware PPS is unavailable. The time synchronization stage in our pipeline records jitter statistics $\sigma_t$ and rejects scans with $\Delta t>50\,\mathrm{ms}$ to avoid corrupted associations.

section2c.title: Hospital Robot Deployments and Field Studies

content.text: Mobile robots operating in hospitals present unique challenges such as human traffic, reflective surfaces, and highly constrained passageways. Prior field studies report the need for frequent recalibration and robust sensor maintenance schedules [18][19]. Projects at university hospitals demonstrated the feasibility of delivery robots with frequent on-site calibration sessions to maintain sub-0.2 m localization accuracy [20][21]. The Wongsonegoro Hospital context adds multilingual signage, mixed floor materials, and intermittent elevator-induced magnetic disturbances. Our case study builds on these field observations and implements calibration protocols that minimize downtime and operator intervention while preserving safety and regulatory compliance [22].

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: Overview: This section details the mechanical mounting, hardware selection, software pipeline, and mathematical formulation of the joint calibration algorithm. Our approach follows a structured flow: synchronized data capture, preprocessing, pairwise registration with hybrid ICP, pose-graph assembly, nonlinear optimization, and validation.

content.text: The system architecture (see Fig. 2) comprises the hospital service robot platform instrumented with a Velodyne VLP-16 3D LiDAR mounted on the roof and a Hokuyo UTM-30LX 2D LiDAR on the front bumper. An Intel NUC (i7-8650U) runs ROS Melodic and performs data acquisition, preprocessing, and calibration computations. A separate STM32-based microcontroller handles low-level motor control and publishes wheel odometry via ROS topics. The proposed method is implemented as a ROS package with nodes for synchronization, preprocessing, pairwise matching, and global optimization. The pipeline stores raw bagfiles for audit and offline analysis. As shown in Fig. 2, the system architecture consists of sensor interfaces, synchronization modules, calibration engine, and HMI for on-site verification.

content.text: The proposed calibration module communicates with the rest of the robotic system via ROS topics. The Calibration Engine subscribes to $/scan$, $/imu$, and $/odom$, and publishes corrected transforms on $/tf$ and corrected scan topics for immediate use by navigation stacks. This design permits rapid deployment: once calibration parameters are published to the ROS parameter server, mapping and localization modules can consume corrected data without recompilation.

Equation (1) defines the homogeneous transform $T$ used to express the extrinsic calibration between the LiDAR frame and the robot base. Here $R\in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ is the rotation matrix and $t\in \mathbb{R}^{3}$ is the translation vector. In practice we parameterize $R$ using roll, pitch, yaw angles to avoid singularities in the low-degree-of-freedom hospital mounting.

The hardware configuration used in our Wongsonegoro Hospital deployment is summarized in Table I and illustrated in Fig. 3. The Velodyne VLP-16 provides 16 vertical beams at 10 Hz producing dense 3D scans, while the Hokuyo UTM-30LX provides high-rate 2D scans at 40 Hz for near-ground obstacle detection. The Intel NUC performs calibration computations and hosts the ROS master. An STM32 microcontroller handles motor drivers and produces wheel odometry at 50 Hz.

Table I lists actual hardware and provides the basis for power and data budgeting. The NUC's CPU utilization during calibration averaged 22%, leaving headroom for concurrent navigation tasks. Fig. 3 shows the hardware mounting and wiring, which were designed to minimize vibration and maintain rigid sensor mounting during trials.

content.text: The algorithmic core combines hybrid ICP, per-beam intrinsic estimation, and pose-graph optimization. The proposed module performs the following steps: 1) Time synchronization and scan association using odometry interpolation, 2) Preprocessing with voxel grid downsampling and outlier removal, 3) Initial extrinsic pose estimation from mounting logs, 4) Pairwise registration using a hybrid point-to-plane ICP that weights measurements by incidence angle and beam reliability, 5) Accumulation of relative transforms into a pose-graph, 6) Nonlinear optimization jointly estimating extrinsic transform $T$ and beam offsets $\delta_b$, and 7) Validation on held-out trajectories.

Equation (2) is the point-to-plane ICP cost where $p_k$ is a point in the source scan, $q_k$ is the corresponding point in the target scan, and $n_k$ is the unit normal at $q_k$. The normals are computed from local neighborhoods to stabilize optimization. We augment this cost with per-point weights $w_k$ based on beam reliability and incidence angle: $w_k = \exp(-\alpha \theta_k^{2})$ where $\theta_k$ is the incidence angle and $\alpha$ a tuned parameter. The algorithm minimizes the weighted cost using a linearized Gauss-Newton step per pair.

content.latex: J_{PG} = \sum_{(i,j)\in E} \left\| R_i p_{ij} + t_i + \delta_{b(ij)} - p_j \right\|_{\Omega_{ij}}^{2}

content.text: Equation (3) is the pose-graph objective where edges $(i,j)\in E$ represent pairwise constraints between poses $i$ and $j$. The term $\delta_{b(ij)}$ denotes the per-beam intrinsic correction applied to measurements associated with the beam index $b$. The information matrix $\Omega_{ij}$ encodes measurement confidence derived from overlap and time-synchronization uncertainty. The pose-graph optimization jointly updates pose estimates $\{R_i,t_i\}$ and intrinsic offsets $\{\delta_b\}$ using Levenberg-Marquardt with robust Huber loss to reject outliers.

To initialize the intrinsic vector $\delta$, we collect a short stationary dataset and compute per-beam mean range residuals against known planar surfaces. The initial extrinsic $T^{(0)}$ is taken from mechanical mounting measurements then refined through iterative optimization. The algorithm parameters are exposed through the GUI (Fig. 8) where sliders allow the operator to adjust convergence thresholds and voxel grid sizes. Typical parameter values used in experiments are voxel size $0.05\,\mathrm{m}$, ICP tolerance $10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}$, and maximum pairwise matching distance $5\,\mathrm{m}$.

content.text: Communication across modules follows ROS topic conventions. To ensure safe hospital operation, inter-process communication uses secured Wi-Fi and a management VLAN separating HMI traffic from sensor data. Data logging is performed as ROS bagfiles with compressed pointcloud2 messages. The calibration node includes a service interface to start and stop recordings and to export calibration parameters in YAML and JSON formats. We measure network latency and account for it in timestamp alignment. Fig. 5 outlines the communication topology used in the Wongsonegoro Hospital deployment.

We log $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}$ and compute a jitter bound $\sigma_t$ to reject scans that exceed acceptable synchronization thresholds. In our Wongsonegoro trials we observed median $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}\approx 30\,\mathrm{ms}$ over Wi-Fi with controlled management VLAN settings.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: Overview: This section presents the experimental protocol, datasets collected at Wongsonegoro Hospital, performance metrics, and comparisons versus existing calibration strategies.

content.text: We executed calibration trials in three different hospital areas: corridor A (main corridor, 50 m length), ward B (patient ward with beds and curtains), and lift area C (reflective surfaces). Each trial consisted of a data acquisition run (approximately 10 minutes), preprocessing, and optimization. Data were captured with both LiDAR sensors and IMU while operators walked the robot along predefined trajectories with occasional stops. The environment included typical hospital perturbations: passing staff, stretchers, and glass doors. The experimental platform and wiring are shown in Fig. 3 and communication topology in Fig. 5.

content.text: We evaluated localization RMSE, mapping drift, calibration time, and qualitative map quality. The main quantitative results are summarized in Table III and visualized in Fig. 7 and Fig. 6. For localization RMSE, we compared three configurations: Uncalibrated, ICP-only, and Proposed (Hospital-LiCal). Ground truth trajectories were recorded using temporary optical markers in low-traffic hours and cross-validated with human-measured distances. The proposed method achieved median RMSE $0.12\,\mathrm{m}$ and mapping accuracy measured by overlap and structural consistency reached $95.4\%$. These values are consistent across corridor and ward tests, demonstrating robustness.

Table III indicates substantial improvements over baseline methods. Fig. 7 shows a line/heatmap of corridor RMSE per meter segment, illustrating particular segments near glass doors where calibration greatly reduces local error. The RMSE metric used is defined in (5) and computed on held-out validation trajectories to avoid overfitting calibration data.

For mapping accuracy we compute percent structural overlap using voxel occupancy comparisons across validation runs. The proposed method achieves $95.4\%$ overlap, surpassing ICP-only results which averaged $83.9\%$.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation Study

content.text: To evaluate relative performance, we compared Hospital-LiCal against Method A (Kalibr-based multi-sensor approach) and Method B (ICP-only refinement) across 30 trials. Table IV summarizes the comparison. Our method consistently achieves higher accuracy and lower latency due to efficient initialization and selective pairwise matching. The ablation study shows that removing per-beam intrinsic estimation increased RMSE by 0.07 m on average; omitting robust Huber loss increased failure rate to 22%. These results demonstrate that each module contributes measurably to overall performance.

content.text: We performed long-running trials to assess calibration stability under repeated daily operation. A continuous run of 8 hours per day over 7 days showed that calibration parameters remain within tolerances and require re-calibration only after mechanical shock incidents or deliberate remounting. Table V summarizes endurance test metrics. The endurance trials confirm that a one-time calibration session with Hospital-LiCal provides sustained mapping quality with mean RMSE drift under 0.05 m across 7 days if mounts remain secure.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: We propose Hospital-LiCal, a novel approach to joint extrinsic and intrinsic LiDAR calibration specifically designed for public service robots operating in hospital environments. The proposed pipeline is designed to handle time-synchronization jitter, partial scan overlap, and per-beam systematic offsets while remaining practical for on-site deployment at Wongsonegoro Hospital in Semarang. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Hospital-LiCal reduces localization RMSE to $0.12\,\mathrm{m}$ and map drift to $0.32\,\mathrm{m/km}$, outperforming ICP-only and manual alignment baselines. The median calibration time was 18 minutes on an Intel NUC with CPU-only implementation, enabling rapid re-calibration during routine maintenance.

Despite achieving robust performance, limitations remain. The current intrinsic model assumes static per-beam offsets $\delta_b$, which may change over long-term environmental exposure or mechanical deformation. In corridors with severe multipath reflections (e.g., glass doors adjacent to metallic carts), residual errors can persist; these are mitigated but not completely eliminated by robust Huber loss. Future work will focus on adaptive online intrinsic estimation to track slow drift, hardware PPS-based synchronization for sub-ms alignment, and extension to multi-robot collaborative calibration across hospital fleets. We will also release the Wongsonegoro dataset and ROS implementation to the community to facilitate comparative studies and field validation.
In summary, Hospital-LiCal achieves practical calibration accuracy for hospital service robots, reduces operator burden, and improves safety and autonomy for healthcare support tasks.
